title: A Rubik's cube that charges a phone?!
_stepChain: a cube has 6 faces → solar panel → 9 × 6 = 54 → milliamps (flow, like a tap) → volts (push) → series adds push → parallel adds flow → battery saves energy → booster makes exactly 5 volts → the pieces turn: contacts, springs, magnets, slip ring → predict 6 lines × 60 = 360 (a line of 9 adds push, not flow) → the contradiction: it barely charged → why (sun angle, gaps) → engineers test for the real number

talk.ask: Why didn't the cube charge the phone much?
talk.goodAnswer: even with sun on every panel, the 6 lines only make 360 milliamps, and a phone wants about 1,000; really the sun only reaches 1 to 3 faces, there are gaps, and not every contact touches, so it made about 200.

talk.ask: What's the difference between series and parallel?
talk.goodAnswer: series is in a line, one after another, like train carriages: the push (volts) adds up. Parallel is side by side, like taps filling one bath: the flow (milliamps) adds up.

talk.ask: How does electricity get between pieces that turn?
talk.goodAnswer: springy metal balls press on metal contacts, magnets keep pieces lined up, and a slip ring passes electricity through the spinning middle.

handsOn: Shine a torch at a box from one side. How many faces get light at once? Then try it with a cube from your Lego.

narration.text: Ismaeel, look at this! It's a Rubik's cube. But it's covered in shiny dark squares. Guess what they do? They catch sunshine, and turn it into electricity! A square that does that is called a solar panel. And this cube can charge a phone. Whoa!
Let's count the solar panels. Each side of the cube has 9. And a cube has 6 sides.

question.onRight: Yes! 6 sides, 9 on each. 6 lots of 9 is 54!

0.mistake: added 9 and 6 instead of 6 lots of 9
0.hint: Every face has its own 9 panels. How many lots of 9 are there?
0.say: Ooh, close. You added 9 and 6. But every side has its own 9! Let's count in nines: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54.

2.hint: Don't forget the top and the bottom of the cube.
2.say: 36 is only the 4 sides you can see around the edge. Don't forget the top and the bottom! 36, 45, 54.

question.reveal: 54 solar panels! 9 on each of the 6 sides.

retry.prompt: Here's a smaller cube, with 4 panels on each side. How many altogether?
retry.onRight: Yes! 6 sides with 4 on each is 24.

0.hint: Every face has its own 4 panels. How many faces are there?
0.say: You added 4 and 6. Count 4 for each of the 6 sides: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.

2.hint: Don't forget the top and the bottom.
2.say: 16 is the 4 sides around the edge. Now add the top and the bottom: 20, 24.

narration.text: Now, a secret about electricity. It's made of tiny, tiny bits, far too small to see. When sunshine hits a panel, the bits zoom out along the wire. Zoom, zoom, zoom! How many bits rush past at once is called the flow. Like a tap! A little flow is a dribble. A big flow is a gush! We measure the flow in milliamps. One panel makes about 60 milliamps.

Electricity needs one more thing: a push. Squeeze a water bottle gently, and the water only dribbles out. Squeeze it hard, and whoosh! It shoots out. That push is called volts. Now here are all 54 panels, laid out flat, so we can see the wires.

On each side, the 9 panels hold hands in a line, one after another, like train carriages. Each panel adds its own push. So the push gets bigger and bigger! Joining them in a line like this is called series.

Then the 6 lines are joined side by side. Imagine 6 taps all pouring into one bath. Splash! Side by side, the flow adds up. More bits rushing at once! This is called parallel. Remember: electricity isn't really water. But thinking of water helps us picture the push and the flow.
Tap a part of the picture, and I'll tell you what it does.

parts.label: Line of 9
parts.narration: 9 panels in a line, like train carriages. In a line, the push adds up.

parts.label: Side by side
parts.narration: 6 lines side by side, like 6 taps into one bath. Side by side, the flow adds up.

parts.label: Battery
parts.narration: All the electricity flows into the battery, to be saved.

narration.text: Where does all that electricity go? Into batteries, hidden right in the middle of the cube! A battery is like a lunchbox for electricity. Fill it up now, and use it later. The maker even designed their own cube on a computer, and printed it on a 3D printer, so the middle was big and hollow. Smart building!

A phone is fussy. It wants a push of exactly 5 volts. Not more, not less. So a tiny chip changes the battery's push to exactly 5 volts. That chip is called a booster. And the plug for the phone? It's hidden under the white middle square. Sneaky!

Now here's the really tricky bit. Even grown-up engineers scratch their heads at this one. Watch the cube turn. Twist! Every piece moves. So how can electricity jump from one moving piece to the next?

Let's peek inside one piece. Where metal touches metal, electricity can cross over. That's called a contact. This cube has 96 springy metal balls, pressing on contacts. Tap each part to find out what it does.

parts.label: Springy balls
parts.narration: Springy metal balls push against the contacts, boing! So electricity can cross, even while the cube is turning.

parts.label: Magnets
parts.narration: Magnets pull the pieces back into line, click! So the contacts touch again.

parts.label: Slip ring
parts.narration: In the middle, a slip ring lets electricity flow through the spinning centre, without the wires getting tangled up.

narration.text: Time for a big sum! Remember: in a line of 9, the push adds up, but the flow stays the same. So each line makes 60 milliamps of flow. And there are 6 lines side by side. Let's pretend the sun is shining on every single panel.

question.prompt: 6 lines, each with a flow of 60 milliamps. How much flow altogether?
question.onRight: Yes! Side by side, the flow adds up. 6 lots of 60 is 360!

0.mistake: added 6 and 60 instead of 6 lots of 60
0.hint: Each of the 6 lines makes its own 60. How many lots of 60 is that?
0.say: You added 6 and 60. But every line makes its own 60! Count in sixties: 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 360.

2.mistake: multiplied all 54 panels by 60, as if every panel were side by side
2.hint: When panels are in a line, which one adds up: the push, or the flow?
2.say: That's a tricky trap! 3,240 is every panel times 60. But in a line, only the push adds up. The flow of a whole line stays at 60. So it's 6 lines of 60: 360.

question.reveal: 360 milliamps, even with sunshine on every panel. But a phone wants about 1,000! That's why the batteries help. They save up electricity all day long.

narration.text: Now the real test! The maker put the cube out in the sunshine, and plugged in a phone. Ready?

question.prompt: Do you think the phone charged quickly?
question.onRight: Good thinking! Our sum pretended the sun was shining on every panel. Let's see what really happened.

0.mistake: trusts the sum without checking what it pretended
0.hint: Our sum pretended the sun shines on every panel. Can the sun shine on all 6 sides at the same time?
0.say: That's what our sum said! But our sum pretended the sun shines on every single panel. Let's see what really happened.

question.reveal: Uh oh. It barely charged at all! Let's find out why.

narration.text: Look where the sun is. It can only reach 1, 2 or 3 sides at once. The other sides are in shadow. Plus there are gaps between the pieces, and the contacts didn't always touch. So the real flow was only about 200 milliamps, and it kept stopping. A phone wants about 1,000. So it barely charged! But that's how engineers learn: they test, and find the real number.

rule.text: Build it. Test it. Find the real number.
rule.ask: What do engineers do? Say it out loud! Then tap the eye to check.
rule.spoken: Engineers build it, test it, and find out the real number.

bonus.prompt: Bonus! If the sun shines on 3 sides, how many panels get sunshine?

0.hint: Each face in the sun has 9 panels. How many lots of 9?
0.say: You added 9 and 3. But each sunny side has 9 panels! Count in nines: 9, 18, 27.

2.hint: Count the faces in the sun again: 3 faces, 9 on each.
2.say: 18 is only 2 sides. Count 3 sides of 9: 9, 18, 27.

_source: requests/videos/videoplayback (transcript checked 2026-11-22): 54 cells, ~1.5 V and 60 mA each in full sun; 9 per face in series, 6 faces in parallel; charge controller + batteries in a hollow 3D-printed core; a chip makes 5 V for a USB-C port under the white centre; 96 brass ball bearings on springs press on brass bolt heads; magnets; slip rings for the spinning centres; real output indoors ~160 mA, in sun 'upwards of only a couple hundred' mA and inconsistent; a phone wants over 1,000 mA.
